nodes.title: Structure of 1 + 2GR(2^n, r)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 3 and r ≥ 1, S = GaloisRing 2 n r. Then 1 + 2S ≅ (ZMod 2^{n−1})^{r−1} × ZMod 2^{n−2} × ZMod 2 as abelian groups (for r = 1: (ZMod 2^n)^× ≅ ZMod 2 × ZMod 2^{n−2}, generated by −1 and 5).

proofSteps: Case r = 1 (Goresky–Klapper Proposition 4.2.1): 5 has order 2^{n−2} since 5^{2^{n−3}} ≡ 1 + 2^{n−1} mod 2^n, and −1 is not a power of 5 mod 4; the product ⟨−1⟩⟨5⟩ has 2^{n−1} elements.

General r: the truncated exponential a ↦ exp(4a) is an isomorphism (S/2^{n−2}S, +) ≅ 1 + 4S, and 1 + 2S/(1 + 4S) ≅ (S/2S, +) = F_{2^r}; the isomorphism type is then fixed by counting, for each k, the elements of 1 + 2S of order dividing 2^k (a finite abelian 2-group is determined by these counts). This counting step is recorded as a gap: the source states the result without proof and refers to McDonald's book, which is not public.

nodes.title: The Frobenius automorphism of GR(p^n, r)
nodes.statement: For p prime and n, r ≥ 1, the Frobenius σ : GaloisRing p n r ≃+* GaloisRing p n r is the automorphism induced, by functoriality of truncated Witt vectors, from the Frobenius automorphism x ↦ x^p of GaloisField p r; equivalently it is the truncation of the Witt vector Frobenius (mathlib:WittVector.frobenius_eq_map_frobenius). It satisfies σ(τ(a)) = τ(a^p), acts on Teichmüller expansions by a_i ↦ a_i^p, reduces to the field Frobenius, fixes exactly the image of ZMod (p^n), and σ^r = id.
hypotheses: p prime; n, r ≥ 1.
proofSteps: Define σ by applying the Witt functor to frobeniusAlgEquivOfAlgebraic / frobenius of GaloisField p r (a ring automorphism of a finite field) and truncating; its inverse comes from the inverse field automorphism.
σ ∘ τ = τ ∘ (·)^p: teichmuller is natural (WittVector.map_teichmuller).
σ^r = id: the field Frobenius has order r on GaloisField p r (FiniteField.frobenius_pow with card p^r).
Fixed ring: by p-adic-expansion-in-galois-ring, σ(x) = x iff every coordinate satisfies a^p = a, i.e. a ∈ ZMod p, iff x lies in the image of ZMod (p^n).
acceptance: σ = id when r = 1.
In GaloisRing 2 2 2, σ has order exactly 2.

nodes.title: The automorphism group of GR(p^n, r) is cyclic of order r
nodes.statement: Let p be prime and n, r ≥ 1. Reduction to the residue field is a group isomorphism (GaloisRing p n r ≃+* GaloisRing p n r) ≃* (GaloisField p r ≃+* GaloisField p r); hence the ring automorphism group of GaloisRing p n r (all of which are ZMod p^n-algebra automorphisms) is cyclic of order r, generated by the Frobenius σ.
hypotheses: p prime; n, r ≥ 1.
proofSteps: Every ring automorphism φ preserves 𝔪 (the non-units) and the Teichmüller set T = {x : x^{p^r} = x}, and commutes with p-adic expansions, so φ(∑ τ(a_i)p^i) = ∑ τ(φ̄(a_i))p^i where φ̄ is the residue automorphism; hence reduction is injective.
Surjectivity: the residue automorphisms are the powers of the field Frobenius (Gal(F_{p^r}/F_p) cyclic of order r), realised by σ^k (frobenius-of-galois-ring).
A ring automorphism fixes the image of ℤ, hence of ZMod p^n, so it is a ZMod p^n-algebra automorphism.
acceptance: Aut(ZMod p^n) is trivial (r = 1).
Aut(GaloisRing 2 2 2) has exactly two elements.

nodes.title: GR(p^n, r) ≅ (ℤ/p^n)[X]/(f) for a monic basic irreducible f of degree r
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, n, r ≥ 1 and f ∈ (ZMod (p^n))[X] monic basic irreducible of degree r. Then there is a ZMod (p^n)-algebra isomorphism AdjoinRoot f ≃ₐ GaloisRing p n r; in particular GaloisRing p n r is free of rank r over ZMod (p^n) with basis 1, α, …, α^{r−1} for any root α of f, and α is a unit.
hypotheses: p prime; n, r ≥ 1; f monic, basic irreducible (basic-irreducible-polynomial), natDegree f = r.
proofSteps: The reduction f̄ ∈ F_p[X] is irreducible of degree r, so it divides X^{p^r} − X and splits with distinct roots in GaloisField p r (GaloisField is the splitting field of X^{p^r} − X; irreducible polynomials over a finite field are separable).
Choose a root ā of f̄; f′(ã) is a unit for any lift ã, so finite-local-ring-is-henselian (with galois-ring-is-local) gives a root α ∈ GaloisRing p n r of f lifting ā.
AdjoinRoot.lift sends the class of X to α: a ZMod (p^n)-algebra map φ : AdjoinRoot f → GaloisRing p n r.
Surjective: the image contains α, and 1, ā, …, ā^{r−1} span GaloisField p r over F_p, so image + 𝔪 = everything; 𝔪 = p·GR is nilpotent, so image = GR (Nakayama for a nilpotent ideal).
Both sides have p^{nr} elements (AdjoinRoot.powerBasis' for monic f over ZMod p^n: free of rank r; galois-ring card), so φ is bijective.

nodes.title: Uniqueness of the unramified extension of ℤ/p^n of degree r
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, n, r ≥ 1 and S a finite commutative local ring containing ZMod (p^n) (an injective ring map), whose maximal ideal is p·S and whose residue field has p^r elements. Then S ≃+* GaloisRing p n r (as ZMod (p^n)-algebras).
hypotheses: p prime; n, r ≥ 1; S finite local, ZMod (p^n) → S injective, 𝔪_S = p·S, #(S/𝔪_S) = p^r.
proofSteps: Pick h ∈ S whose residue generates S/𝔪_S over F_p (a primitive element of the finite residue field) and let f be the monic lift of its minimal polynomial obtained as ∏ over the orbit of h under the ring automorphisms fixing ZMod p^n — or, more simply, lift the minimal polynomial ḡ of h̄ to a monic g ∈ ZMod(p^n)[X] and replace h by the unique root of g lifting h̄ (finite-local-ring-is-henselian).

g is monic basic irreducible of degree r; AdjoinRoot g → S, X ↦ h, is surjective by Nakayama (𝔪_S = pS nilpotent) and |S| = p^{nr} (S is a free ZMod p^n-module since 𝔪_S = pS: the length of S is n·r).
Hence S ≅ AdjoinRoot g ≅ GaloisRing p n r by galois-ring-presentation.

nodes.title: The ideals of GR(p^n, r) form the chain (p^i)
nodes.statement: Let p be prime and n, r ≥ 1. Every ideal of GaloisRing p n r equals p^i · GaloisRing p n r for a unique 0 ≤ i ≤ n, and GaloisRing p n r ⧸ (p^m) ≃+* GaloisRing p m r for m ≤ n (via truncation).
hypotheses: p prime; n, r ≥ 1.
proofSteps: A nonzero x has a first nonzero Teichmüller coordinate a_i (p-adic-expansion-in-galois-ring), so x = p^i u with u a unit (u has nonzero 0-th coordinate; galois-ring-is-local); hence every ideal is generated by p^{i} for i the least such index among its elements.
The kernel of truncation to length m is (p^m) (coordinates of p^m: WittVector.coeff_p_pow_eq_zero and coeff_p_pow).

nodes.title: Galois subrings of GR(p^n, r) are the GR(p^n, e), e ∣ r
nodes.statement: Let p be prime and n, r ≥ 1, S = GaloisRing p n r with Frobenius σ. For each e ∣ r the fixed subring S^{σ^e} is isomorphic to GaloisRing p n e, and e ↦ S^{σ^e} is an inclusion-reversing bijection from the divisors of r to the subrings R' ⊆ S that are local with maximal ideal p·R' (equivalently, the subrings that are Galois extensions of ZMod p^n). Not every subring is of this form: for r = 2, n = 2 the subring ZMod 4 + 2S has 8 elements.
hypotheses: p prime; n, r ≥ 1; e ∣ r.
proofSteps: S^{σ^e} is a finite local ring with maximal ideal p·S^{σ^e} (fixed points of an automorphism of a local ring whose Teichmüller coordinates are fixed coordinatewise) and residue field F_{p^e}; by galois-ring-uniqueness it is GaloisRing p n e.

Conversely a subring R' local with 𝔪 = pR' has residue field a subfield F_{p^e} of F_{p^r}; R' contains the Teichmüller lifts of that subfield (they are the roots of X^{p^e} − X lifting it, unique by finite-local-ring-is-henselian) and is generated by them over ZMod p^n, so R' = S^{σ^e}.
The counterexample: ZMod 4 + 2·GaloisRing 2 2 2 is closed under multiplication, contains 1 and has 4·4/2 = 8 elements, while GaloisRing 2 2 e has 4 or 16 elements.
acceptance: The Galois subrings of GaloisRing 3 2 6 are GaloisRing 3 2 e for e ∈ {1, 2, 3, 6}.

nodes.title: Trace of GR(p^n, r) over ℤ/p^n: Galois sum, surjectivity, duality
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, n, r ≥ 1, S = GaloisRing p n r, R = ZMod (p^n). (a) Algebra.trace R S x = ∑_{k<r} σ^k(x), and residue ∘ Tr_{S/R} = Tr_{F_{p^r}/F_p} ∘ residue. (b) Tr_{S/R} is surjective. (c) For every R-linear L : S → R there is a unique b ∈ S with L(x) = Tr_{S/R}(bx) for all x; b is a unit iff L is surjective.
hypotheses: p prime; n, r ≥ 1; S is free of rank r over R (galois-ring-presentation), so Algebra.trace is defined as a matrix trace.
proofSteps: (a) Both sides are R-linear; they agree modulo 𝔪 by the finite-field formula (mathlib:FiniteField.algebraMap_trace_eq_sum_pow), and the set where two R-linear maps S → R agree is a submodule N with N + 𝔪S = S, so N = S by Nakayama (Goresky–Klapper Lemma 4.4.3).
(b) The residue of the trace is the field trace, which is surjective; pick c with Tr(c) a unit and scale (Corollary 4.4.4).

(c) b ↦ (x ↦ Tr(bx)) is R-linear and injective (if Tr(bx) = 0 for all x and b = p^m u with u a unit, m < n, then p^m Tr(x) = 0 for all x, contradicting surjectivity); both sides have |R|^r elements (Theorem 4.4.6(4)).
acceptance: For r = 1, Tr is the identity of ZMod p^n.

nodes.title: q-linearized (additive) polynomials
nodes.statement: Let K be a commutative semiring and q a natural number. A polynomial L ∈ K[X] is q-linearized (a q-polynomial), written Polynomial.IsLinearized q L, if every exponent in its support is a power of q, i.e. L = ∑_i a_i X^{q^i}. The constructor linearizedOf q a := ∑_i C (a i) · X^{q^i} turns a finitely supported coefficient sequence a : ℕ →₀ K into a q-polynomial; its q-degree is the largest i with a_i ≠ 0. Convention (pinned): exponents are q^i with i ≥ 0, so X = X^{q^0} is linearized and nonzero constants are not; q ≥ 2 in every theorem.
hypotheses: K is a commutative semiring for the definition; the linearity theorems assume K is a field of characteristic p and q = p^e with e ≥ 1.
proofSteps: Define IsLinearized q L :↔ ∀ n ∈ L.support, ∃ i, n = q^i.
Closure under +, under multiplication by constants and under finite sums is immediate from Polynomial.support_add ⊆ and support_C_mul ⊆.

linearizedOf q a is linearized because each monomial C c · X^{q^i} has support ⊆ {q^i}; conversely every linearized L equals linearizedOf q (fun i ↦ L.coeff (q^i)) since i ↦ q^i is injective for q ≥ 2.
Composition closure and linearity of evaluation are separate nodes (linearized-polynomial-comp, linearized-polynomial-eval-linear).
acceptance: X^q − X, X and 0 are q-linearized; X² + X is 2-linearized over ZMod 2; X² + 1 and X³ are not 2-linearized.

sources.excerpt: Then a polynomial of the form L(x) = ∑_{i=0}^{n} a_i x^{q^i} = a0x + a1x^q + · · · + anx^{q^n} ∈ F_{q^m}[x] is called a q-polynomial over F_{q^m}. Such polynomials are also known as linearised polynomials

nodes.title: Evaluation of a q-polynomial is F_q-linear
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, q = p^e (e ≥ 1), F a finite field with q elements, K an F-algebra that is a field, E a commutative K-algebra, and L ∈ K[X] q-linearized. Then x ↦ aeval x L is additive on E and satisfies L(c·x) = c·L(x) for c ∈ F; hence it is an F-linear map IsLinearized.toLinearMap : E →ₗ[F] E.
hypotheses: F finite with Fintype.card F = q = p^e; CharP K p; E a commutative K-algebra (so of characteristic p).
proofSteps: (x + y)^{q^i} = x^{q^i} + y^{q^i} in a commutative ring of characteristic p (iterated frobenius, add_pow_char_pow); sum over the monomials of L.
For c ∈ F, c^{q} = c (FiniteField.pow_card), so (c x)^{q^i} = c^{q^i} x^{q^i} = c x^{q^i}; multiply by the coefficient and sum.
acceptance: For L = X^q − X and E = F itself, toLinearMap is the zero map.
For L = X² + X over ZMod 2 and E = GaloisField 2 2, toLinearMap has kernel {0, 1}.

sources.excerpt: (1) L(β + γ) = L(β) + L(γ) for all β, γ ∈ F_{q^m}, (2) L(cβ) = cL(β) for all c ∈ F_q, β ∈ F_{q^m}. We remark that properties (1) and (2) hold more generally for β, γ in an arbitrary extension field of F_{q^m}.

nodes.title: q-polynomials are closed under composition
nodes.statement: Let K be a commutative ring of characteristic p and q = p^e with e ≥ 1. If L₁ = ∑ a_i X^{q^i} and L₂ = ∑ b_j X^{q^j} are q-linearized, then L₁.comp L₂ is q-linearized with L₁ ∘ L₂ = ∑_k (∑_{i+j=k} a_i b_j^{q^i}) X^{q^k}; composition is associative and distributes over addition on both sides, so the q-polynomials form a (noncommutative) ring under + and ∘ with unit X.
hypotheses: CharP K p, q = p^e, e ≥ 1.
proofSteps: (∑_j b_j X^{q^j})^{q^i} = ∑_j b_j^{q^i} X^{q^{i+j}} by additivity of the q^i-th power map in characteristic p (Polynomial.expand and frobenius on K[X]).
Multiply by a_i and sum over i; collect by k = i + j.

Left distributivity L ∘ (M + N) = L ∘ M + L ∘ N uses the additivity of evaluation of L (linearized-polynomial-eval-linear applied in the K-algebra K[X]); right distributivity and associativity hold for all polynomials (Polynomial.add_comp, Polynomial.comp_assoc).
acceptance: (X^q) ∘ (a X) = a^q X^q and (a X) ∘ X^q = a X^q: composition is not commutative unless a^q = a.
(X^q − X) ∘ (X^q − X) = X^{q²} − 2X^q + X.

sources.excerpt: Note that (ax^i)(bx^j) = ab^{q^i}x^{i+j} is mapped to ab^{q^i}x^{q^{i+j}} = (ax^{q^i}) ◦ (bx^{q^j}).

nodes.title: The roots of a q-polynomial form an F_q-subspace
nodes.statement: In the setting of linearized-polynomial-eval-linear (F finite with q elements, K an F-algebra field of characteristic p, E a field extension of K), for L ∈ K[X] q-linearized the set of roots of L in E is the F-subspace LinearMap.ker (IsLinearized.toLinearMap L) of E; if L ≠ 0 it is finite.
hypotheses: F finite, Fintype.card F = q = p^e; E a field with [Algebra K E]; L q-linearized.
proofSteps: The roots in E are the zeros of the F-linear map x ↦ L(x) (linearized-polynomial-eval-linear), i.e. its kernel.
Finiteness for L ≠ 0: a nonzero polynomial has finitely many roots in a field (Polynomial.rootSet is finite).
acceptance: The roots of X^q − X in any extension E of F are exactly the image of F.
X² + X over ZMod 2 has root set {0, 1} in GaloisField 2 2, a 1-dimensional F₂-subspace.

sources.excerpt: It is widely known that the roots of any linearized polynomial form a subspace in some extension of F_{q^n} (seen as a vector space over F_q)
sources.match: The theorem.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1. [15, Theorem 3.50, p. 108] If P is a linearized polynomial whose splitting field is F_{q^n}, then each root of P in F_{q^n} has the same multiplicity, which is a non-negative power of q, and the roots form a linear subspace of F_{q^n}.
sources.match: The subspace clause; the multiplicity clause is node linearized-polynomial-separable-iff.

nodes.title: A q-polynomial is separable iff its coefficient of X is nonzero
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic p, q = p^e (e ≥ 1) and L = ∑_{i≤m} a_i X^{q^i} ∈ K[X] q-linearized and nonzero. (a) L is separable iff a_0 ≠ 0. (b) If a_0 ≠ 0 and L splits over a field E ⊇ K, then L has exactly q^m distinct roots in E, where m is the q-degree. (c) If K is perfect and t is the least index with a_t ≠ 0, every root of L in a splitting field has multiplicity exactly q^t.
hypotheses: CharP K p; q = p^e, e ≥ 1; L ≠ 0; (c) assumes PerfectField K.
proofSteps: The derivative of X^{q^i} is q^i X^{q^i − 1} = 0 for i ≥ 1 in characteristic p, so L′ = a_0 (Polynomial.derivative).
(a) If a_0 ≠ 0, L′ is a nonzero constant, so IsCoprime L L′ (mathlib:Polynomial.separable_def); if a_0 = 0 then L′ = 0 and L (nonconstant) is not separable.
(b) A separable split polynomial has natDegree many distinct roots (mathlib:Polynomial.card_rootSet_eq_natDegree), and natDegree L = q^m.

(c) Over a perfect field L = M^{q^t} with M = ∑_i a_i^{1/q^t} X^{q^{i−t}} (take q^t-th roots of the coefficients; frobenius is bijective), and M has nonzero X-coefficient, so M is separable by (a); each root of L is a simple root of M, hence of multiplicity q^t in L.
acceptance: X^q − X is separable (a_0 = −1) with exactly q roots in F_q.
X^{q²} + X^q = (X^q + X)^q over F_q is not separable and each root has multiplicity q.

nodes.title: The subspace polynomial of a finite F_q-subspace
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements, E a field with [Algebra F E], and U a finite F-subspace of E (a Submodule F E with Finite U). Its subspace polynomial is P_U := ∏_{u ∈ U} (X − C u) ∈ E[X]. It is monic of degree #U = q^{dim U}, separable, its roots in E are exactly U, and it is q-linearized (node subspace-polynomial-is-linearized).
hypotheses: F finite, Fintype.card F = q; U a finite-dimensional F-subspace of the field E (finite since F is finite).
proofSteps: Define P_U := ∏_{u ∈ U.toFinset} (X − C u) (Finset.prod over the finite carrier).
Monic of degree #U: product of monic linear factors (Polynomial.monic_prod_of_monic, natDegree_prod).
Roots = U with multiplicity one: roots of a product of distinct linear factors (Polynomial.roots_prod_X_sub_C); hence separable (Polynomial.nodup_roots converse for split polynomials).
#U = q^{finrank F U} (Module.card_eq_pow_finrank).
acceptance: For U = the image of F in E, P_U = X^q − X (FiniteField.roots_X_pow_card_sub_X).

sources.excerpt: A monic linearized polynomial P with coefficients in F_{q^n} is called a subspace polynomial with respect to F_{q^n} if the following equivalent conditions hold: 1) P divides x^{[n]} − x. 2) P splits completely over F_{q^n} and all its roots have multiplicity 1.

nodes.title: Subspace polynomials are q-linearized
nodes.statement: In the setting of subspace-polynomial, P_U is q-linearized for every finite F-subspace U ⊆ E; its coefficient of X is nonzero and its q-degree is dim_F U. Conversely every monic q-linearized L ∈ E[X] with nonzero X-coefficient that splits over E is the subspace polynomial of its root space.
hypotheses: F finite with q elements; U a finite-dimensional F-subspace of the field E.
proofSteps: Induction on dim U. For U = ⊥, P_U = X.

If U = U′ ⊕ F·w with w ∉ U′, then P_U(X) = ∏_{c ∈ F} P_{U′}(X − c w) = ∏_{c ∈ F} (P_{U′}(X) − c P_{U′}(w)), using that P_{U′} is linearized (induction) and hence additive and F-linear as a polynomial map in the K-algebra E[X] (linearized-polynomial-eval-linear).

∏_{c ∈ F}(Y − c b) = Y^q − b^{q−1} Y for b ∈ E (the roots of Y^q − b^{q−1}Y are the c b; FiniteField.roots_X_pow_card_sub_X scaled), so P_U = P_{U′}^q − P_{U′}(w)^{q−1} P_{U′}, a q-linearized polynomial by linearized-polynomial-comp.

The X-coefficient is nonzero since P_U is separable (subspace-polynomial) and linearized-polynomial-separable-iff; the converse follows from roots-of-linearized-polynomial and linearized-polynomial-separable-iff (b), comparing monic polynomials with the same simple roots.
acceptance: For U = F₂·1 + F₂·a ⊆ GaloisField 2 2 (a² = a + 1), P_U = X⁴ + X.
For U = F·w of dimension one, P_U = X^q − w^{q−1} X.

nodes.title: The linearized q-associate of a polynomial
nodes.statement: Let K be a commutative semiring and q ∈ ℕ. The linearized q-associate of l = ∑_i a_i X^i ∈ K[X] is linearizedAssociate q l := ∑_i a_i X^{q^i} (Lidl–Niederreiter call l the conventional q-associate of this linearized polynomial). The map l ↦ linearizedAssociate q l is additive and injective for q ≥ 2, and when K = F is a finite field with q elements it turns multiplication into composition: linearizedAssociate q (l * m) = (linearizedAssociate q l).comp (linearizedAssociate q m); hence (F[X], +, ·) ≅ (q-polynomials over F, +, ∘) and, modulo X^n − 1 ↦ X^{q^n} − X, F[X]/(X^n − 1) ≅ L_n(F).
hypotheses: q ≥ 2; the multiplicativity statement requires the coefficients to lie in a finite field F with exactly q elements (so a^q = a).
proofSteps: Define linearizedAssociate q := Polynomial.sum with C a * X^(q^i) (an additive map K[X] →+ K[X]); its image is the set of q-linearized polynomials (linearized-polynomial, eq_linearizedOf).
Multiplicativity on monomials: (a X^{q^i}) ∘ (b X^{q^j}) = a b^{q^i} X^{q^{i+j}} = a b X^{q^{i+j}} for b ∈ F (linearized-polynomial-comp and FiniteField.pow_card); extend biadditively.
linearizedAssociate q (X^n − 1) = X^{q^n} − X, giving the quotient statement.
acceptance: linearizedAssociate q (X − 1) = X^q − X and linearizedAssociate q 1 = X.
Over F₄ ⊋ F₂ (q = 2) and a ∉ F₂, (C a * X).comp (X^2) ≠ (X^2).comp (C a * X): multiplicativity needs coefficients in F_q.

sources.excerpt: As to the subalgebra Ln(F_{q^m}), in [15] Ore derived that Ln(F_q) ≅ F_q[x]/(x^n − 1)
sources.match: The quotient isomorphism; the map is the q-associate correspondence.

nodes.title: A q-polynomial permutes F_{q^m} iff 0 is its only root there
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements, E a finite field extension of F, and L ∈ E[X] q-linearized. Then x ↦ L(x) is a bijection of E iff the only root of L in E is 0.
hypotheses: F finite with q elements; E a finite field with [Algebra F E].
proofSteps: x ↦ L(x) is F-linear (linearized-polynomial-eval-linear); an injective endomorphism of a finite set is bijective, and a linear map is injective iff its kernel is 0 (roots-of-linearized-polynomial).
acceptance: X^q − X does not permute E (every element of F is a root).
Over F₄ = GaloisField 2 2 the 2-polynomial X² + X has the nonzero root 1, so it does not permute F₄, while X² (Frobenius) does.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.15. Let F_q be of characteristic p. Then the p-polynomial L(x) = ∑_{i=0}^{m} a_i x^{p^i} ∈ F_q[x] is a PP if and only if L(x) only has the root 0 in F_q.
sources.match: The theorem, for q-polynomials over F_{q^m}.

nodes.title: The associate gcd criterion for q-polynomials with coefficients in F_q
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements, m ≥ 1, E a field extension of F of degree m, and l = ∑_{i<m} a_i X^i ∈ F[X]. Then linearizedAssociate q l permutes E iff gcd(l, X^m − 1) = 1 in F[X].
hypotheses: F finite with q elements; [E : F] = m ≥ 1; natDegree l < m.
proofSteps: Write L = linearizedAssociate q l and g = gcd(l, X^m − 1) = a·l + b·(X^m − 1) (Bézout in F[X]). By linearized-q-associate, assoc(g) = assoc(a) ∘ L + assoc(b) ∘ (X^{q^m} − X), and X^{q^m} − X vanishes on E (FiniteField.pow_card with #E = q^m); hence every root of L in E is a root of assoc(g).
Conversely g ∣ l gives L = assoc(l/g) ∘ assoc(g), so every root of assoc(g) is a root of L. Thus the roots of L in E are the roots of assoc(g) in E.
If g = 1 then assoc(g) = X, whose only root is 0, and L permutes E by linearized-permutation-root-criterion.

If deg g ≥ 1: g(0) ≠ 0 since g ∣ X^m − 1, so assoc(g) is separable (linearized-polynomial-separable-iff) with q^{deg g} > 1 roots in its splitting field; each root y satisfies y^{q^m} = y (because X^{q^m} − X = assoc(h) ∘ assoc(g) with g·h = X^m − 1), so all lie in E, and L has a nonzero root in E: not a permutation.
acceptance: For l = 1 + X (q = 2, m = 2): gcd(1 + X, X² − 1) = X + 1 ≠ 1, and indeed X² + X kills F₂ ⊂ F₄.
For l = X^k, X^{q^k} is a field automorphism of E, and gcd(X^k, X^m − 1) = 1.

nodes.title: Dickson's matrix criterion for linearized permutation polynomials
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements, E ⊇ F of degree m, and L = ∑_{i<m} a_i X^{q^i} ∈ E[X]. Let D_L ∈ M_m(E) be the Dickson matrix with entries (D_L)_{i,j} = a_{(j−i) mod m}^{q^i}. Then the F-linear map x ↦ L(x) of E has rank equal to rank D_L and determinant equal to det D_L (which lies in F); in particular L permutes E iff det D_L ≠ 0.
hypotheses: F finite with q elements; [E : F] = m ≥ 1; indices of a read modulo m.
proofSteps: For an F-basis (β_j) of E and its trace-dual basis, the matrix M_L of x ↦ L(x) satisfies M_L = B^{−1} D_L B with B = (β_j^{q^i}) (Wu–Liu Lemma 4.2): from (L(x)^{q^i})_i = D_L (x^{q^j})_j, since L(x)^{q^i} = ∑_j a_{j−i}^{q^i} x^{q^j}.
B is invertible (Moore/Vandermonde-type matrix of a basis; its nonsingularity is equivalent to linear independence of the β_j over F).
Similar matrices have the same rank and determinant (Wu–Liu Proposition 4.3); combine with linearized-permutation-root-criterion.
acceptance: For L = X (a_0 = 1, other a_i = 0), D_L is the identity.
For L = X^q − X on E of degree m = 2, D_L = [[−1, 1], [1, −1]] is singular.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 4.3. For any L(x) ∈ Ln(F_{q^n}), rk L = rk D_L and det L = det D_L, where rk L and det L are the rank and determinant, respectively, of the linear transformation induced by L(x).
sources.match: The theorem.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 4.3 is a direct generalization of Dickson’s well known criterion on linearized permutation polynomials, which concludes that a linearized polynomial is a permutation polynomial if and only if the Dickson matrix associated to it is non-singular
sources.match: The permutation corollary.

nodes.title: Permutation polynomials of a finite field
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements. A polynomial f ∈ F[X] is a permutation polynomial of F, written IsPermutationPolynomial f, if the evaluation map x ↦ f.eval x is a bijection F → F. Equivalent forms (Shallue Lemma 1.3): injective; surjective; f(x) = a solvable for every a. The property depends only on f mod (X^q − X) (Shallue Lemma 1.2), and there are exactly q! permutation polynomials of degree < q.
hypotheses: F is a finite field; Fintype.card F = q.
proofSteps: Define IsPermutationPolynomial f := Function.Bijective (fun x : F ↦ f.eval x).
Injective ↔ surjective ↔ bijective for self-maps of a finite type (mathlib:Finite.injective_iff_bijective, Finite.surjective_iff_bijective).
f and f %ₘ (X^q − X) agree on F since X^q − X vanishes on F (FiniteField.pow_card), so the property depends only on the reduction.

Counting: evaluation is a bijection from polynomials of degree < q to functions F → F (Lagrange interpolation, Lagrange.interpolate; uniqueness from Polynomial.eq_zero_of_natDegree_lt_card_of_eval_eq_zero'); the bijections number q!.
acceptance: x³ + 1 permutes ZMod 11 (Shallue Example 1.2); x² + 3x + 5 does not (Example 1.3).
Composition of permutation polynomials is a permutation polynomial.

sources.excerpt: Definition 1.1. A polynomial f ∈ F_q[x] is called a Permutation Polynomial (PP) of F_q if the associated polynomial function f : c → f(c) is a permutation of F_q.
sources.match: The definition.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 1.2. For any f, g ∈ F_q[x] we have f(c) = g(c) for all c ∈ F_q if and only if f(x) ≡ g(x) mod (x^q − x).
sources.match: Dependence on the reduction.

sources.excerpt: If q is a prime power then there are exactly q! PPs of F_q of degree < q.
sources.match: The count.

nodes.title: Power sums detect enumerations of F_q
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements and a : Fin q → F. Then a is a bijection iff ∑_i a_i^t = 0 for 0 ≤ t ≤ q − 2 and ∑_i a_i^{q−1} = −1.
hypotheses: F finite, q = Fintype.card F; 0^0 = 1 (Mathlib's convention), so t = 0 gives ∑ 1 = q = 0 in F.
proofSteps: ⇒: reindex by the bijection and use ∑_{x∈F} x^t = 0 for t < q − 1 (mathlib:FiniteField.sum_pow_lt_card_sub_one) and ∑_{x∈F} x^{q−1} = q − 1 = −1 (every nonzero x has x^{q−1} = 1, mathlib:FiniteField.pow_card_sub_one_eq_one).

⇐ (Shallue's proof): g(x) := −∑_{t<q} (∑_i a_i^t) x^{q−1−t} has degree ≤ q − 1 and equals the indicator of the value set {a_i}; the hypotheses force g = 1, so the value set is F; a surjection Fin q → F with #F = q is a bijection.
acceptance: Any enumeration of ZMod 5 has ∑ a_i² = 0 and ∑ a_i⁴ = −1.
The constant sequence a_i = 0 fails at t = q − 1 (sum 0 ≠ −1).

sources.excerpt: Lemma 1.4. The sequence a0, ..., aq−1 of elements of F_q satisfies {a0, ..., aq−1} = F_q if and only if ∑_{i=0}^{q−1} a_i^t = 0 for t = 0, 1, ..., q − 2, and −1 for t = q − 1.
sources.match: The lemma.

nodes.title: The X^{q−1}-coefficient of a reduction mod X^q − X is minus the value sum
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements and g ∈ F[X]. The coefficient of X^{q−1} in g %ₘ (X^q − X) equals −∑_{c∈F} g(c).
hypotheses: F finite, q = Fintype.card F ≥ 2.
proofSteps: g and its reduction r agree on F (Shallue Lemma 1.2) and deg r ≤ q − 1; by the Carlitz interpolation formula r = ∑_c g(c)(1 − (X − c)^{q−1}) (both sides have degree ≤ q − 1 and agree on F), whose X^{q−1}-coefficient is −∑_c g(c).
Uniqueness of the interpolant: mathlib:Polynomial.eq_zero_of_natDegree_lt_card_of_eval_eq_zero'.
acceptance: For g = X^{q−1}: the reduction is X^{q−1} with coefficient 1 = −(q − 1).
For g = 1 the coefficient is 0 = −q.

sources.locator: Chapter 1, proof of Theorem 1.5, printed p. 10
sources.excerpt: For each 1 ⩽ t ⩽ q − 1, denote the reduction of f(x)^t modulo x^q − x by f(x)^t mod (x^q − x) = ∑_{i=0}^{q−1} b^{(t)}_i x^i. Note that by (1.1) we have b^{(t)}_{q−1} = −∑_{c∈F_q} f(c)^t.
sources.match: The lemma, applied to g = f^t.
The Carlitz interpolation formula.

nodes.title: Hermite's criterion
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q = p^r elements and f ∈ F[X]. Then f is a permutation polynomial of F iff (1) the reduction f^{q−1} %ₘ (X^q − X) has degree q − 1 (equivalently: is monic of degree q − 1), and (2) for every t with 1 ≤ t ≤ q − 2 and p ∤ t, the reduction f^t %ₘ (X^q − X) has degree ≤ q − 2.
hypotheses: F finite of characteristic p with q elements, q ≥ 2.
proofSteps: By top-coefficient-of-reduction the X^{q−1}-coefficient of f^t %ₘ (X^q − X) is −∑_c f(c)^t.
⇒: power-sums-detect-enumerations applied to (f(c))_c gives the coefficient conditions.
⇐: (2) gives ∑_c f(c)^t = 0 for p ∤ t, and t = t′p^j reduces to t′ since the p^j-th power is additive; (1) gives ∑_c f(c)^{q−1} = −1; t = 0 is trivial; conclude by power-sums-detect-enumerations.
acceptance: q = 5, f = X³: condition (2) at t = 1, 2, 3 and (1) hold (X³ permutes F₅ since gcd(3, 4) = 1).
q = 5, f = X²: t = 2 gives X⁴ of degree 4 = q − 1, violating (2).

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.5. (Hermite’s criterion.) Let q = p^r, where p is a prime and r is a positive integer. Then a polynomial f ∈ F_q[x] is a PP of F_q if and only if the following two conditions hold: (1) the reduction of f(x)^{q−1} mod (x^q − x) is monic of degree q − 1;
sources.match: The theorem; the remark after the proof allows 'degree q − 1' in place of 'monic of degree q − 1'.

nodes.title: Hermite's criterion with exactly one root
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q = p^r elements and f ∈ F[X]. Then f is a permutation polynomial of F iff (1) f has exactly one root in F, and (2) for every t with 1 ≤ t ≤ q − 2 and p ∤ t, the reduction f^t %ₘ (X^q − X) has degree ≤ q − 2.
hypotheses: F finite of characteristic p with q elements, q ≥ 2.
proofSteps: ⇒: a bijection has exactly one root; (2) holds by hermite-criterion.
⇐: if f has exactly j = 1 root then ∑_c f(c)^{q−1} = q − 1 = −1, so the X^{q−1}-coefficient of f^{q−1} %ₘ (X^q − X) is 1 (top-coefficient-of-reduction) and hermite-criterion applies.
Only this implication is needed: the converse 'coefficient 1 ⇒ exactly one root' asserted in the source's proof is false for non-prime q (source issue E502).
acceptance: X^4 − 1 over GaloisField 3 2 (q = 9) has four roots, yet the X⁸-coefficient of (X⁴ − 1)⁸ mod X⁹ − X is −(9 − 4) = 1 in F₉: the step 'coefficient 1 iff exactly one root' fails, while the theorem is unaffected.
Every linear polynomial aX + b with a ≠ 0 satisfies (1) and (2).

sources.locator: Chapter 1, Theorem 1.6 and proof, printed pp. 10–11
sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.6. Let q = p^r, where p is a prime and r is a positive integer. Then a polynomial f ∈ F_q[x] is a PP of F_q if and only if the following two conditions hold: (1) f has exactly one root in F_q;
sources.match: The theorem; its proof is corrected (E502).

nodes.title: Character-sum criterion for permutation polynomials
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field and f ∈ F[X]. Then f is a permutation polynomial of F iff ∑_{c∈F} ψ(f(c)) = 0 for every nontrivial additive character ψ : AddChar F ℂ.
hypotheses: F finite; characters with values in ℂ.
proofSteps: ⇒: reindex the sum by the bijection f and use ∑_x ψ(x) = 0 for ψ ≠ 1 (mathlib:AddChar.sum_eq_zero_of_ne_one).

⇐: for a ∈ F, the number of c with f(c) = a is (1/q) ∑_ψ ∑_c ψ(f(c) − a) (orthogonality, mathlib:AddChar.sum_eq_ite applied to the dual group, which has q elements for a finite field); the hypothesis leaves only the trivial character's contribution q/q = 1.
acceptance: For f = X² on F₅ and ψ(x) = e(x/5), ∑_c ψ(c²) is the quadratic Gauss sum √5 ≠ 0.
For f = X + 1 every character sum vanishes.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.9. A polynomial f ∈ F_q[x] is a PP of F_q if and only if ∑_{c∈F_q} χ(f(c)) = 0 for all nontrivial additive characters χ of F_q.
sources.match: The theorem.

nodes.title: X^n permutes F_q iff gcd(n, q − 1) = 1
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements and n ≥ 1. Then X^n is a permutation polynomial of F iff Nat.Coprime n (q − 1).
hypotheses: F finite; n ≥ 1 (for n = 0, X^0 = 1 is not a permutation when q ≥ 2).
proofSteps: 0^n = 0, so X^n permutes F iff x ↦ x^n permutes Fˣ.

Fˣ is cyclic of order q − 1; the n-th power map on a finite group of order N is bijective when gcd(n, N) = 1 (mathlib:powCoprime), and when g = gcd(n, q − 1) > 1 its kernel contains a nontrivial g-th root of unity (a generator raised to (q − 1)/g).
acceptance: X³ permutes ZMod 11 (gcd(3, 10) = 1); X² does not.
X^q permutes F (gcd(q, q − 1) = 1): it is the identity map.

sources.locator: Chapter 1, Theorem 1.14(2) and proof, printed p. 14
sources.excerpt: (2) The monomial x^n is a PP of F_q if and only if gcd(n, q − 1) = 1.
sources.match: The theorem.

nodes.title: No permutation polynomial of degree n > 1 with n ∣ q − 1
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements and n ≥ 2 with n ∣ q − 1. Then no polynomial of natDegree n is a permutation polynomial of F.
hypotheses: n ≥ 2 (the source omits this hypothesis; for n = 1 the claim is false — source issue E504).
proofSteps: Write q − 1 = n m; n ≥ 2 gives 1 ≤ m ≤ q − 2, and p ∤ m since m ∣ q − 1.
f^m has degree nm = q − 1 < q, so it is its own reduction, of degree q − 1 > q − 2, violating condition (2) of hermite-criterion at t = m.
acceptance: No quadratic polynomial permutes a finite field of odd order.
Linear polynomials are permutation polynomials although 1 ∣ q − 1, which is why n ≥ 2 is required.

sources.excerpt: Corollary 1.8. If q ≡ 1 mod n then there is no PP of F_q of degree n.
sources.match: The theorem with the missing hypothesis n ≥ 2 added (E504).

nodes.title: Dickson polynomials of the first kind: D_n(u + a/u, a) = u^n + (a/u)^n
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring, a ∈ R and x, y ∈ R with x·y = a. Then for every n, (dickson 1 a n).eval (x + y) = x^n + y^n, where dickson 1 a n is Mathlib's n-th Dickson polynomial of the first kind with parameter a (dickson 1 a 0 = 2, dickson 1 a 1 = X, D_{n+2} = X D_{n+1} − a D_n). In particular D_n(x, 0) = x^n for n ≥ 1.
hypotheses: R commutative; no invertibility is needed (the form u + a/u is recovered with x = u, y = a/u when u is a unit).
proofSteps: Two-step induction on n with the recurrence (mathlib:Polynomial.dickson_add_two): x^{n+2} + y^{n+2} = (x + y)(x^{n+1} + y^{n+1}) − xy(x^n + y^n) and xy = a.
Base cases: dickson 1 a 0 = 3 − 1 = 2 = x^0 + y^0 (mathlib:Polynomial.dickson_zero) and dickson 1 a 1 = X (mathlib:Polynomial.dickson_one).
This generalises mathlib:Polynomial.dickson_one_one_eval_add_inv (the case a = 1).
acceptance: D_2(x, a) = x² − 2a: with x·y = a, (x + y)² − 2a = x² + y².
a = 0, y = 0: D_n(x, 0) = x^n for n ≥ 1.

sources.excerpt: There is a more general definition of Dickson polynomial of the first kind that depends on a parameter a. In the more general definition, Dk(x, a) is determined by the formula Dk(u + a/u, a) = u^k + (a/u)^k.
sources.match: The lemma for general a.

sources.excerpt: Dickson polynomials satisfy a number of interesting properties, for example we have g1(x, a) = x, g2(x, a) = x^2 − 2a, and gk+1(x, a) = xgk(x, a) − agk−1(x, a), for k ⩾ 2.
sources.match: The recurrence identifying Shallue's g_k(x, a) with dickson 1 a k.

nodes.title: Every x ∈ F_q is u + a/u with u ∈ F_q^× or u^{q+1} = a
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements, a ∈ F^× and L a quadratic extension of F (e.g. GaloisField p (2r) when q = p^r). For every x ∈ F there is u ∈ L^× with x = u + a/u, and then either u ∈ F^× (u^{q−1} = 1) or u^{q+1} = a; conversely u + a/u ∈ F whenever u^{q−1} = 1 or u^{q+1} = a. Moreover u + a/u = v + a/v iff v ∈ {u, a/u}.
hypotheses: F finite with q elements; a ≠ 0; L ⊇ F with [L : F] = 2.
proofSteps: x = u + a/u iff u² − xu + a = 0; this quadratic splits in L, and its roots are nonzero since their product is a.
x ∈ F iff x^q = x iff u^q + a/u^q = u + a/u iff (u^q − u)(1 − a/u^{q+1}) = 0, i.e. u^q = u or u^{q+1} = a (computation with the Frobenius of L/F).
u + a/u = v + a/v ⟺ (uv − a)(u − v) = 0 (clear denominators).
acceptance: For q = 3, a = 1, x = 0: u² + 1 = 0 has no root in F₃ (−1 is a nonsquare there); its roots in F₉ have order 4, so u^{q+1} = u⁴ = 1 = a.

sources.locator: Section 2, Lemma 2.1 and proof, printed p. 5
sources.excerpt: It has been noted in [4], [8, Lemma 3.5], and [6, p. 356] that u+1/u ∈ F_q iff u^{q+1} = 1 or u^{q−1} = 1.
sources.match: The case a = 1; the node generalises to a ∈ F^× with u^{q+1} = a.

sources.excerpt: If uv ≠ 0, then ⟨u⟩ = ⟨v⟩ ⇐⇒ u^2v + v = uv^2 + u ⇐⇒ (uv − 1)(u − v) = 0, and so ⟨u⟩ = ⟨v⟩ ⇐⇒ v ∈ {u, 1/u}.
sources.match: The fibre description (a = 1).

nodes.title: Dickson's theorem: D_n(x, a) permutes F_q iff gcd(n, q² − 1) = 1
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements, a ∈ F^× and n ≥ 1. Then the Dickson polynomial dickson 1 a n is a permutation polynomial of F iff Nat.Coprime n (q² − 1). For a = 0, dickson 1 0 n = X^n permutes F iff Nat.Coprime n (q − 1) (monomial-permutation-criterion).
hypotheses: F finite with q elements; n ≥ 1; the main statement needs a ≠ 0.
proofSteps: Parametrise F by dickson-parametrisation: F = {u + a/u : u ∈ μ_{q−1}} ∪ {u + a/u : u ∈ A}, A = {u ∈ L : u^{q+1} = a}.

By dickson-functional-equation D_n(u + a/u) = u^n + (a/u)^n = u^n + a^n/u^n; D_n maps the first part via u ↦ u^n on μ_{q−1} (parameter a^n, still in F) and the second via u ↦ u^n on the coset A (u^{n(q+1)} = a^n).

If gcd(n, q² − 1) = 1 then u ↦ u^n is injective on L^× (order q² − 1, mathlib:powCoprime) and, with the fibre description of dickson-parametrisation (u + a/u = v + a/v iff v ∈ {u, a/u}, and a/u^n corresponds to (a/u)^n), D_n is injective on F; injective on a finite set means bijective.

Conversely compute the image as in Bluher Proposition 2.4: with r = gcd(n, q − 1) and s = gcd(n, q + 1), u ↦ u^n maps μ_{q−1} onto μ_{(q−1)/r} (r-to-1) and the coset A onto the corresponding coset for a^n (s-to-1), and u ↦ u + a/u is exactly 2-to-1 off the at most two points with u² = a; counting the image gives #D_n(F) < q unless r = s = 1, i.e. unless gcd(n, q² − 1) = 1 (for q odd, gcd(n, q−1) = gcd(n, q+1) = 1 iff gcd(n, q² − 1) = 1 since q² − 1 = (q − 1)(q + 1); for q even the two factors are coprime).
acceptance: D_5(x, 1) = x⁵ − 5x³ + 5x permutes F₇ (gcd(5, 48) = 1): its values at 0, …, 6 are 0, 1, 2, 4, 3, 5, 6.
D_3(x, 1) = x³ − 3x does not permute F₅ since 3 ∣ 24 = 5² − 1, although gcd(3, 5 − 1) = 1 (so X³ does permute F₅): the parameter a ≠ 0 changes the criterion.

nodes.title: The least period of a purely periodic sequence
nodes.statement: For a type α let seqShift : (ℕ → α) → (ℕ → α), (seqShift s) n = s (n + 1). The least period of s : ℕ → α is seqLeastPeriod s := Function.minimalPeriod seqShift s: the least T ≥ 1 with s (n + T) = s n for all n, and 0 (Mathlib's junk value) when s is not purely periodic. A sequence is eventually periodic if some shift seqShift^[k] s is purely periodic; its preperiod is the least such k.
hypotheses: α arbitrary; no finiteness needed for the definition.
proofSteps: seqShift^[T] s = s ↔ ∀ n, s (n + T) = s n (Function.iterate_succ_apply and funext), so Function.IsPeriodicPt seqShift T s is the usual periodicity.
Divisibility: every period is a multiple of the least period (mathlib:Function.IsPeriodicPt.minimalPeriod_dvd); the least period is a period (mathlib:Function.isPeriodicPt_minimalPeriod).
Positivity iff purely periodic: mathlib:Function.minimalPeriod_pos_iff_mem_periodicPts.
acceptance: The sequence 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, … over ZMod 2 has least period 3.
1, 0, 0, 0, … is eventually periodic with preperiod 1 but has seqLeastPeriod 0.

sources.excerpt: A sequence a = (a0, a1, · · · ) is periodic if there exists T > 0 so that ai = ai+T for all i ≥ 0. Such a T is called a period of the sequence a and the least such T is called the period, or sometimes the least period of a.
sources.match: The definition; Mathlib's minimalPeriod of the shift map realises 'least such T'.

sources.excerpt: But for any periodic sequence, every period is some multiple of the minimal period.

nodes.title: The order (period, exponent) of a polynomial over a finite field
nodes.statement: Let F be a field and f ∈ F[X]. The order of f is polyOrder f := orderOf (AdjoinRoot.root f), the multiplicative order of the class of X in F[X]/(f). For f with f(0) ≠ 0 over a finite field it is the least e ≥ 1 with f ∣ X^e − 1; if f(0) = 0 (or f = 0 over an infinite field) the value is the junk 0. Pinned: the order of a constant nonzero polynomial is 1.
hypotheses: F a field; the positivity and divisibility statements assume F finite.
proofSteps: Define polyOrder f := orderOf (AdjoinRoot.root f) in the monoid AdjoinRoot f.
root^e = 1 in AdjoinRoot f ↔ f ∣ X^e − 1 (AdjoinRoot.mk_eq_mk / AdjoinRoot.mk_eq_zero); hence f ∣ X^e − 1 ↔ polyOrder f ∣ e (orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one).

For F finite and f(0) ≠ 0 the root is a unit of the finite ring AdjoinRoot f (X is invertible modulo f since gcd(X, f) = 1), so its order is positive and divides #(AdjoinRoot f)ˣ (orderOf_dvd_card); for f irreducible of degree m, AdjoinRoot f is a field with q^m elements and polyOrder f ∣ q^m − 1.
For irreducible f and a root α in any field extension L, F[X]/(f) ≅ F(α) sends root to α, so polyOrder f = orderOf α.
The reverse polynomial X^m f(1/X) has the same order (Goresky–Klapper Lemma 6.1.5: f g = X^N − 1 gives f* g* = ±(X^N − 1)).
acceptance: polyOrder (X⁴ + X + 1) = 15 and polyOrder (X⁴ + X³ + X² + X + 1) = 5 over ZMod 2.
polyOrder ((X + 1)²) = 2 over ZMod 2, since (X + 1)² = X² + 1.

sources.locator: Chapter 3, Section 3.2, proof of Theorem 3.2.1, printed p. 65
sources.excerpt: Recall that in the terminology of Section 2.4.a, the order of f is the smallest T such that f(x)|(x^T −1). This is the order of x in the group of units of F[x]/(f), a group that has |F|^{deg(f)} −1 elements.
sources.match: The definition as the order of the class of x; the node records the junk value 0 when x is not a unit.

nodes.title: Primitive polynomials over a finite field
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements. A polynomial f ∈ F[X] is a primitive polynomial, IsPrimitivePoly f, if f is monic and irreducible of degree m ≥ 1 and the class of X generates the cyclic group (F[X]/(f))ˣ, i.e. polyOrder f = q^m − 1. Equivalently: f is the minimal polynomial over F of a generator of the multiplicative group of the field with q^m elements. Name pinned as IsPrimitivePoly because Mathlib's Polynomial.IsPrimitive means content 1.
hypotheses: F finite with q elements; m = natDegree f ≥ 1.
proofSteps: Define IsPrimitivePoly f := f.Monic ∧ Irreducible f ∧ 1 ≤ f.natDegree ∧ polyOrder f = q^(f.natDegree) − 1.

Characterisation (Goresky–Klapper Lemma 3.2.10): for monic f with f(0) ≠ 0, polyOrder f = q^m − 1 already forces irreducibility, because for a reducible f the order of X modulo f is bounded by the lcm of the orders modulo the factors, which is < q^m − 1 (the unit group of F[X]/(f) then has order < q^m − 1).
Minimal polynomials of generators: if γ generates (GaloisField p (r m))ˣ, minpoly F γ is monic irreducible of degree m with polyOrder = orderOf γ = q^m − 1 (order-of-polynomial).

Count: generators of a cyclic group of order q^m − 1 number φ(q^m − 1), each primitive polynomial has m roots, all generators (the Frobenius conjugates), so there are φ(q^m − 1)/m primitive polynomials of degree m.
acceptance: X⁴ + X + 1 is primitive over ZMod 2; X⁴ + X³ + X² + X + 1 is irreducible but not primitive.
Over ZMod 5, X − 2 is primitive (2 generates F₅ˣ) and X − 4 is not.

sources.excerpt: A polynomial f ∈ Fp[x] of degree d is primitive if it is irreducible and if one (and hence all) of its roots in F_{p^d} are primitive elements.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 3.2.10. Let F = F_q be the field with q elements. Let f ∈ F[x] be a polynomial. Then f is primitive if and only if its order is q^{deg(f)} −1.

nodes.title: Linear recurring sequences over a finite ring are eventually periodic
nodes.statement: Let R be a finite commutative ring and E : LinearRecurrence R of order m (Mathlib: u(n + m) = ∑_{i<m} c_i u(n + i)). Every solution u is eventually periodic. If the coefficient c_0 is a unit (equivalently the characteristic polynomial E.charPoly has unit constant coefficient), every solution is purely periodic: 0 < seqLeastPeriod u.
hypotheses: R finite commutative; m ≥ 0 (for m = 0 the only solution is 0).
proofSteps: The state vector s_n = (u(n), …, u(n + m − 1)) ∈ R^m determines the future (s_{n+1} = A s_n with A the transposed companion matrix; ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/linear-recurrence-as-a-matrix-power), and R^m is finite, so s_i = s_j for some i < j; then u(n + j − i) = u(n) for n ≥ i.

If c_0 is a unit, the state map is invertible (det of the companion matrix is ± c_0; CA.2/companion-matrix), so s_i = s_j implies s_0 = s_{j−i}: purely periodic; conclude with least-period-of-sequence.
acceptance: Over ZMod 2 the recurrence u(n + 2) = u(n + 1) + u(n) has purely periodic solutions of period dividing 3.
The recurrence u(n + 1) = 0·u(n) (c_0 = 0) has the eventually periodic, not purely periodic, solution 1, 0, 0, ….

sources.excerpt: In particular, LFSR sequences are eventually periodic.
sources.match: The first statement.

sources.excerpt: The LFSR will output strictly periodic sequences if and only if its length m equals the degree of its connection polynomial, that is, if q_m ≠ 0.
sources.match: The pure periodicity statement (over a field; over a ring the unit condition is used).

nodes.title: The period of a linear recurring sequence divides the order of its characteristic polynomial
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field, E : LinearRecurrence F of order m ≥ 1 with charPoly f := E.charPoly satisfying f.coeff 0 ≠ 0, and u a solution. Then u is purely periodic and seqLeastPeriod u ∣ polyOrder f.
hypotheses: F finite field; f(0) ≠ 0 (so polyOrder f > 0).
proofSteps: Let T = polyOrder f, so f ∣ X^T − 1 (order-of-polynomial). The companion matrix A satisfies f(A) = 0 (CA.2/companion-matrix: minpoly of the companion matrix is f), hence A^T = I.
s_T = A^T s_0 = s_0 (CA.2/linear-recurrence-as-a-matrix-power), so T is a period of u, and seqLeastPeriod u ∣ T (least-period-of-sequence).
acceptance: For f = X² + X + 1 over ZMod 2 (order 3) every solution has period 1 or 3.
The zero solution has period 1, which divides every order.

nodes.title: The impulse response has period exactly the order
nodes.statement: In the setting of period-divides-polynomial-order, the impulse-response solution (initial values u(0) = 1, u(1) = ⋯ = u(m − 1) = 0; Mathlib's E.mkSol) has seqLeastPeriod equal to polyOrder E.charPoly.
hypotheses: F finite field; m ≥ 1; E.charPoly has nonzero constant coefficient.
proofSteps: The states s_0 = e_0, s_1, …, s_{m−1} of the impulse response form a basis of F^m (triangular with nonzero diagonal c_0; Goresky–Klapper's argument with the invertible coefficient).

If r is a period of u, A^r fixes s_0 and hence every s_k = A^k s_0, so A^r = I and f ∣ X^r − 1 (f is the minimal polynomial of A, CA.2/companion-matrix); so polyOrder f ∣ r. Combine with period-divides-polynomial-order.
acceptance: Over ZMod 2 with u(n + 4) = u(n + 1) + u(n) (charPoly X⁴ + X + 1, order 15) the impulse response has period 15.
For charPoly X⁴ + X³ + X² + X + 1 the impulse response has period 5.

nodes.title: Trace representation of linear recurring sequences with irreducible characteristic polynomial
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field, E : LinearRecurrence F of order m ≥ 1 whose charPoly f is irreducible, L a field extension of F of degree m and β ∈ L a root of f. Then for every solution u there is a unique A ∈ L with u(n) = Tr_{L/F}(A β^n) for all n; conversely each such sequence is a solution. (In Goresky–Klapper's connection-polynomial convention a_n = T(α^{−n}A) with α = β^{−1} a root of the connection polynomial.)
hypotheses: F finite; f = E.charPoly irreducible of degree m; [L : F] = m; β a root of f in L.
proofSteps: n ↦ Tr(A β^n) solves the recurrence: A β^n f(β) = 0 and Tr is F-linear (Goresky–Klapper Theorem 6.6.4).

The map L → F^m, A ↦ (Tr(A β^i))_{i<m} is injective: if Tr(Aβ^i) = 0 for i < m then Tr(A x) = 0 for all x (1, β, …, β^{m−1} is a basis of L = F(β)), and the trace form is nondegenerate for the separable extension L/F (mathlib:traceForm_nondegenerate), so A = 0.
Both sides have q^m elements, so the map is onto the space of initial values; solutions are determined by initial values (mathlib:LinearRecurrence.eq_mk_of_is_sol_of_eq_init).
acceptance: Fibonacci mod 2 (charPoly X² + X + 1): u(n) = Tr_{F₄/F₂}(A ω^n) with ω² = ω + 1; the solution 0, 1, 1, … has A = 1 (Tr(1) = 0, Tr(ω) = Tr(ω²) = 1).
The zero sequence corresponds to A = 0.

nodes.title: A nonzero solution with irreducible characteristic polynomial has period equal to the order
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field and E : LinearRecurrence F with irreducible charPoly f, f ≠ X. Every nonzero solution u has seqLeastPeriod u = polyOrder f; it divides q^m − 1, m = deg f.
hypotheses: F finite; f irreducible, f ≠ X (so f(0) ≠ 0).
proofSteps: By trace-representation-of-lrs, u(n) = Tr(Aβ^n) with A ≠ 0. If T is a period then Tr(A(β^T − 1)β^n) = 0 for all n, hence A(β^T − 1) = 0 by nondegeneracy of the trace form (as in trace-representation-of-lrs), so β^T = 1 and polyOrder f = orderOf β ∣ T (order-of-polynomial, polyOrder_eq_orderOf).
Conversely polyOrder f is a period (period-divides-polynomial-order).
acceptance: Every nonzero solution of u(n + 4) = u(n + 3) + u(n + 2) + u(n + 1) + u(n) over ZMod 2 (charPoly X⁴ + X³ + X² + X + 1) has period 5.
For the reducible charPoly (X + 1)² over ZMod 2 the solution 1, 1, 1, … has period 1 ≠ 2 = polyOrder: irreducibility is needed.

nodes.title: m-sequences (maximal-length linear recurring sequences)
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements and m ≥ 1. A sequence u : ℕ → F is an m-sequence of degree m, IsMSequence m u, if u ≠ 0 and u solves a linear recurrence E : LinearRecurrence F of order m whose characteristic polynomial E.charPoly is a primitive polynomial (primitive-polynomial). Equivalent (Goresky–Klapper Definition 13.1.1): u is generated by a length-m recurrence and every nonzero block of length m occurs exactly once in each period (node m-sequence-state-cycle).
hypotheses: F finite with q elements; m ≥ 1.
proofSteps: Define IsMSequence m u := u ≠ 0 ∧ ∃ E : LinearRecurrence F, E.order = m ∧ IsPrimitivePoly E.charPoly ∧ E.IsSolution u.
Period: seqLeastPeriod u = polyOrder E.charPoly = q^m − 1 (period-of-irreducible-recurrence and primitive-polynomial).
Trace form: u(n) = Tr(A α^n) with α a generator of the units of the degree-m extension (trace-representation-of-lrs).

Shifts and decimations: seqShift u is an m-sequence (same recurrence); the d-fold decimation n ↦ u(dn) with gcd(d, q^m − 1) = 1 is an m-sequence, with characteristic polynomial the minimal polynomial of α^d (Goresky–Klapper Proposition 13.2.1(2)).
acceptance: The Fibonacci sequence mod 2 is an m-sequence of degree 2 with period 3.
A nonzero solution for X⁴ + X³ + X² + X + 1 over ZMod 2 is not an m-sequence (period 5 < 15).

nodes.title: The states of an m-sequence run through all nonzero vectors
nodes.statement: Let u be an m-sequence of degree m over F (q elements). Then the map n ↦ (u(n), …, u(n + m − 1)), 0 ≤ n < q^m − 1, is a bijection onto F^m \ {0}. Conversely, a sequence generated by a length-m linear recurrence whose states in one period are exactly the nonzero vectors is an m-sequence.
hypotheses: F finite; m ≥ 1.
proofSteps: The state map is conjugate to multiplication by α on L = F_{q^m} via the trace model (trace-representation-of-lrs: A ↦ (Tr(Aα^i))_{i<m} is an F-linear bijection L → F^m), and α generates Lˣ, so the orbit of A ≠ 0 is Lˣ.

Converse (Goresky–Klapper Proposition 13.1.2(1)): the state change is multiplication by x^{−1} on F[x]/(q) (Theorem 6.6.2); cycling through all nonzero states forces every nonzero element to be a power of this element, so F[x]/(q) is a field and the characteristic polynomial is primitive.
acceptance: For the Fibonacci sequence mod 2 the states (0,1), (1,1), (1,0) are the three nonzero vectors of F₂².
For X⁴ + X³ + X² + X + 1 only 5 of the 15 nonzero states occur in a period.

nodes.title: Balance of m-sequences
nodes.statement: Let u be an m-sequence of degree m over F with q elements, period N = q^m − 1. In one period each nonzero c ∈ F occurs exactly q^{m−1} times and 0 occurs exactly q^{m−1} − 1 times. More generally each block b ∈ F^k (1 ≤ k ≤ m) occurs q^{m−k} times, except the zero block, which occurs q^{m−k} − 1 times.
hypotheses: F finite; m ≥ 1; 1 ≤ k ≤ m.
proofSteps: By m-sequence-state-cycle the length-m states in one period are the nonzero vectors, each once; a block of length k is the prefix of q^{m−k} vectors of F^m, all nonzero unless the block is zero, when the zero vector must be removed.
acceptance: The binary m-sequence of period 15 has eight 1s and seven 0s.

nodes.title: The shift-and-add property of m-sequences
nodes.statement: Let u be an m-sequence of degree m over F with period N = q^m − 1, c ∈ F and τ ∈ ℕ. Then the sequence n ↦ u(n) + c·u(n + τ) is either identically zero (exactly when 1 + cα^τ = 0 in the trace model; for c = 1 this means α^τ = −1, i.e. τ ≡ 0 mod N when q is even and τ ≡ N/2 mod N when q is odd) or a shift of u: there is s with u(n) + c·u(n + τ) = u(n + s) for all n.
hypotheses: F finite; m ≥ 1.
proofSteps: With u(n) = Tr(Aα^n), u(n) + c u(n + τ) = Tr(A(1 + cα^τ)α^n); if 1 + cα^τ ≠ 0 it equals α^s for some s since α generates Lˣ, giving u(n + s).
acceptance: For the binary m-sequence of period 15 and τ = 1, u + seqShift u = seqShift^[s] u for a unique s mod 15.
For q = 2, τ = 0: u + u = 0.

nodes.title: Periodic cross-correlation and autocorrelation
nodes.statement: For T ∈ ℕ and complex sequences u v : ℕ → ℂ, periodicCorrelation T u v τ := ∑_{i<T} u(i)·conj(v(i + τ)). For sequences a b : ℕ → G in a finite abelian group G and a character χ : AddChar G ℂ, the correlation with respect to χ is charCorrelation χ T a b τ := periodicCorrelation T (χ ∘ a) (χ ∘ b) τ = ∑_{i<T} χ(a_i − b_{i+τ}), and the autocorrelation is charCorrelation χ T a a. Conventions (pinned): the conjugate is on the second (shifted) argument; the sum runs over one period T supplied explicitly.
hypotheses: T is a period of the sequences in the theorems (the definition does not require it).
proofSteps: Define periodicCorrelation by Finset.sum over Finset.range T.
χ(a) conj χ(b) = χ(a − b) for characters into the unit circle (AddChar.map_neg_eq_conj / AddChar.map_sub_eq_div), giving the character form.
Shift invariance: if u, v have period T then periodicCorrelation T u v (τ + T) = periodicCorrelation T u v τ, and the sum may be taken over any T consecutive indices.
Autocorrelation at 0: periodicCorrelation T u u 0 = ∑ |u i|² = T for unimodular u.
acceptance: For the constant sequence u = 1: periodicCorrelation T u u τ = T for all τ.
For u = (1, −1, 1, −1, …) and T = 2: the autocorrelation at τ = 1 is −2.

sources.excerpt: Definition 11.3.1. The (periodic) cross-correlation function of the sequences a, b with respect to the character χ is the function C_{a,b}(τ) = ∑_{i=0}^{T−1} χ(a_i) χ̄(b_{i+τ}). The (periodic) autocorrelation function A_a(τ) = C_{a,a}(τ) of the sequence a is its cross-correlation with itself.

nodes.statement: Let u be an m-sequence of degree m over F with q elements, N = q^m − 1, and χ : AddChar F ℂ nontrivial. Then charCorrelation χ N u u τ = N if N ∣ τ and = −1 otherwise.
hypotheses: F finite; χ ≠ 1.
proofSteps: N ∣ τ: every term is χ(0) = 1.

Otherwise u(i) − u(i + τ) = Tr(A(1 − α^τ)α^i) with c := A(1 − α^τ) ≠ 0, and i ↦ cα^i runs over Lˣ once per period; so the sum is ∑_{x ∈ Lˣ} χ(Tr x) = ∑_{x∈L} χ(Tr x) − 1 = −1, since χ ∘ Tr is a nontrivial character of L (Tr surjective) and mathlib:AddChar.sum_eq_zero_of_ne_one.
acceptance: Binary m-sequence of period 15, χ(x) = (−1)^x: the autocorrelation is 15, −1, −1, …, −1 (Golomb's third postulate).
For m = 1, q = 5: u(n) = 2^n mod 5 has autocorrelation −1 at τ = 1, 2, 3.

nodes.title: Dirichlet and Legendre sequences
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime, ψ : MulChar (ZMod p) ℂ and c ∈ ℂ. The Dirichlet sequence is dirichletSeq ψ c : ℕ → ℂ, n ↦ c if p ∣ n and ψ(n) otherwise; it has period p. The Legendre sequence of an odd prime p is legendreSeq p := dirichletSeq (quadratic character) 1, with values ±1. Convention (pinned): the value at multiples of p is the explicit parameter c (the source uses c = 0 for Dirichlet sequences and c = 1 for Legendre sequences), never Mathlib's MulChar value ψ(0) = 0 silently.
hypotheses: p prime (odd for Legendre sequences).
proofSteps: Define dirichletSeq ψ c n := if (n : ZMod p) = 0 then c else ψ n.
Periodicity: (n + p : ZMod p) = n.
Legendre values: for n ≢ 0, the quadratic character (quadraticChar (ZMod p), or legendreSym) is ±1.
acceptance: legendreSeq 3 = (1, 1, −1, 1, 1, −1, …) and legendreSeq 5 = (1, 1, −1, −1, 1, …).
dirichletSeq ψ 0 agrees with n ↦ ψ n everywhere (Mathlib's convention ψ(0) = 0).

sources.excerpt: It is customary to extend each Dirichlet character to all of Z/(p) by setting ψ(0) = 0, but there is no “correct” value for ψ(0) and engineers often take ψ(0) = 1 to obtain a sequence of ±1 values.

nodes.title: Autocorrelation of Dirichlet and Legendre sequences
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, ψ a nontrivial multiplicative character of ZMod p with values in ℂ, c ∈ {0, 1}, s = dirichletSeq ψ c and τ with p ∤ τ. Then ∑_{x<p} s(x + τ)·conj(s(x)) = −1 + c·(ψ(τ) + conj ψ(−τ)). For the Legendre sequence (p odd): the autocorrelation at τ ≢ 0 is −1 if p ≡ 3 (mod 4) and −1 + 2·legendre(τ/p) ∈ {1, −3} if p ≡ 1 (mod 4); at τ ≡ 0 it is p (and p − 1 for c = 0).
hypotheses: p prime; ψ ≠ 1; c ∈ {0, 1} (real); p ∤ τ.
proofSteps: Split off x = 0 and x = −τ: the remaining terms are ψ((x + τ)x^{−1}) = ψ(1 + τx^{−1}) for x ∉ {0, −τ}.
As x runs over (ZMod p)ˣ \ {−τ}, y = 1 + τx^{−1} runs over ZMod p \ {0, 1}, so their sum is ∑_{y≠0} ψ(y) − ψ(1) = −1 (character orthogonality, MulChar.sum_eq_zero_of_ne_one).
The boundary terms are ψ(τ)conj(c) + c·conj ψ(−τ). For the quadratic character ψ(−1) = (−1)^{(p−1)/2} (quadraticChar_neg_one / FiniteField.isSquare_neg_one_iff), giving the two Legendre cases.
acceptance: legendreSeq 7 has autocorrelation −1 at every τ ≢ 0 (7 ≡ 3 mod 4).

sources.excerpt: Proposition 14.8.1. Let ψ be a non-trivial Dirichlet character. Let τ ≢ 0 (mod p). Set R = ψ(0)(ψ(τ) + ψ̄(−τ)) … Then the autocorrelation with shift τ of the resulting Dirichlet sequence is A(τ) = −1 + R.
sources.match: The theorem; the value at τ ≡ 0 is corrected (source issue E509).

sources.excerpt: We remark that the quadratic character satisfies ψ(−1) = −1 if and only if p ≡ 3 (mod 4), in which case R = 0.
sources.match: The Legendre case p ≡ 3 mod 4.

nodes.title: Cross-correlation of an m-sequence with its decimation is a character sum
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements, L ⊇ F of degree m, α a generator of Lˣ, a(n) = Tr_{L/F}(α^n) and b(n) = a(dn) its d-fold decimation (d ≥ 1), N = q^m − 1 and χ : AddChar F ℂ. Then for every t, charCorrelation χ N b a t = ∑_{x ∈ L} χ(Tr_{L/F}(x^d − α^t x)) − 1.
hypotheses: F finite; α generates Lˣ; d ≥ 1.
proofSteps: Write the sum over i < N with x = α^i ranging over Lˣ once: χ(b_i) conj χ(a_{i+t}) = χ(Tr(x^d) − Tr(α^t x)) = χ(Tr(x^d − α^t x)) (periodic-correlation, character form).
Add and subtract the x = 0 term, which is χ(0) = 1.
acceptance: d = 1: charCorrelation χ N a a t = ∑_x χ(Tr((1 − α^t)x)) − 1, which is N at t ≡ 0 and −1 otherwise (m-sequence-two-level-autocorrelation).
d = q (a linear decimation): Tr(x^q) = Tr(x), so again −1 for t ≢ 0 (Goresky–Klapper Proposition 13.5.3).

sources.locator: Chapter 13, Proposition 13.5.1 and proof (13.4)–(13.7), printed pp. 318–319
sources.excerpt: The cross-correlation of the sequences a, b with respect to the character χ is given by C_{b,a}(t) = ∑_{x∈E} χ(Tr(x^d − Ax)) −1 (13.2)
sources.match: The lemma with A = α^t.

nodes.title: The Singleton bound for linear codes
nodes.statement: Let F be a field, ι a finite type with n = #ι, and C ≤ F^ι a linear code (TauCeti.LinearCode F ι = Submodule F (ι → F)) with k = finrank F C ≥ 1. Then some nonzero c ∈ C has hammingNorm c ≤ n − k + 1; equivalently, if every nonzero codeword has weight ≥ d then k ≤ n − d + 1.
hypotheses: F a field (finite in the source; not needed); ι finite; k ≥ 1 (for the zero code the statement is vacuous).
proofSteps: Choose any set S ⊆ ι of k − 1 coordinates. The restriction C → F^S has kernel of dimension ≥ k − (k − 1) = 1 (rank–nullity, LinearMap.finrank_range_add_finrank_ker), so some nonzero c ∈ C vanishes on S.
hammingNorm c ≤ n − (k − 1) since c vanishes on the k − 1 coordinates of S (hammingNorm counts nonzero coordinates, mathlib:hammingNorm).
acceptance: The repetition code {(a, …, a)} ≤ F^n (k = 1) meets the bound with weight n.
The binary [7, 4, 3] Hamming code has 3 < 7 − 4 + 1 = 4: the bound is not attained.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 4.3.1 (Singleton Bound). For every (n,k,d)q code, k ≤ n −d +1.
sources.match: The theorem for linear codes, via a dimension count instead of the source's prefix count.

sources.excerpt: they reach Singleton bound [82, Th. 1.11] asserting that for any code of length n and dimension k and minimum distance d, we always have k + d ⩽ n+1.
sources.match: The same bound in the form k + d ≤ n + 1.

nodes.title: Maximum distance separable (MDS) codes
nodes.statement: Let F be a field with decidable equality, ι finite with n = #ι. A linear code C ≤ F^ι is MDS, IsMDS C, if every nonzero codeword c ∈ C has hammingNorm c ≥ n − finrank F C + 1, i.e. its minimum distance equals the Singleton value n − k + 1 (singleton-bound gives the reverse inequality when k ≥ 1). The predicate is stated with Mathlib's hammingNorm so it does not depend on a bundled minimum-distance invariant; with AlgebraicCodingTheory Layer 2's minimum distance d(C) (zero-code convention d(⊥) = 0), a nonzero code is MDS iff d(C) = n − k + 1.
hypotheses: F a field; ι finite; decidable equality on F for hammingNorm.
proofSteps: Define IsMDS C :↔ ∀ c ∈ C, c ≠ 0 → n + 1 ≤ hammingNorm c + finrank F C.
Projection property (ECT Proposition 5.3.3): for S ⊆ ι with #S = k, the restriction C → F^S is injective (a nonzero codeword vanishing on S has weight ≤ n − k), hence bijective by dimension count.

Compatibility with the minimum distance of AlgebraicCodingTheory Layer 2: for C ≠ ⊥ the least weight of a nonzero codeword equals the minimum distance (ACT Layer 2), so IsMDS C ↔ d(C) = n − k + 1 by singleton-bound.
acceptance: Reed–Solomon codes are MDS (reed-solomon-is-mds).
The binary code spanned by (1,1,0,0) and (0,0,1,1) is [4, 2, 2], not MDS.

sources.excerpt: Definition 5.3.1 (MDS codes). An (n,k,d)q code is called Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) if d = n −k +1.
sources.match: The definition.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 5.3.3. Let C ⊆ Σ^n of integral dimension k be an MDS code, then for all S ⊆ [n] such that |S| = k, we have |C_S| = Σ^k.

nodes.title: Reed–Solomon codes
nodes.statement: Let F be a field, ι finite, α : ι → F (the evaluation points) and k ∈ ℕ. The Reed–Solomon code is reedSolomon α k := the image of the evaluation map reedSolomonEncode α k : Polynomial.degreeLT F k →ₗ[F] (ι → F), p ↦ (p.eval (α i))_i. Pinned: messages are polynomials of degree < k identified with F^k by the coefficient basis 1, X, …, X^{k−1} (the Vandermonde generator matrix); the theorems about dimension and distance assume α injective and k ≤ #ι, which forces #ι ≤ #F (the field-size restriction n ≤ q).
hypotheses: F a field; ι a finite coordinate type; α injective and k ≤ #ι in the theorems (not in the definition).
proofSteps: Define reedSolomonEncode α k := (LinearMap.pi fun i ↦ Polynomial.leval (α i)) ∘ₗ (degreeLT F k).subtype and reedSolomon α k := LinearMap.range of it.
Linearity is built in (ECT Claim 5.2.2).
Injectivity for α injective and k ≤ #ι: a polynomial of degree < k vanishing at #ι ≥ k distinct points is zero (mathlib:Polynomial.eq_zero_of_natDegree_lt_card_of_eval_eq_zero').
Dimension k: injective linear map from degreeLT F k, which has dimension k (mathlib:Polynomial.degreeLTEquiv).
Generator matrix: the k × ι Vandermonde matrix V_{j,i} = α_i^j generates the code (reedSolomon = range V.vecMulLinear), matching TauCeti's Matrix.generatedBy.
Field-size restriction: α injective gives #ι ≤ #F (Fintype.card_le_of_injective).
acceptance: Over F₃ with α enumerating F₃ and k = 2 the code has the nine codewords listed in ECT §5.2.
k = 0 gives ⊥ and k = 1 the repetition code.

sources.excerpt: Definition 5.2.1 (Reed-Solomon code). Let Fq be a finite field, and choose n and k satisfying k ≤ n ≤ q. Fix a sequence α = (α1,α2,...αn) of n distinct elements (also called evaluation points) from Fq.

proofSteps: c = (p(α_i))_i with p ≠ 0 of degree < k; the zero coordinates are the α_i that are roots of p, at most k − 1 of them since α is injective and p has at most natDegree p ≤ k − 1 roots (mathlib:Polynomial.card_roots').

IsMDS: reed-solomon-min-weight.

nodes.title: Generalized Reed–Solomon codes
nodes.statement: For α : ι → F, k ∈ ℕ and a multiplier vector v : ι → F with all v i ≠ 0, the generalized Reed–Solomon code is GRS(α, k, v) := {(v_i p(α_i))_i : deg p < k}, the image of reedSolomon α k under the diagonal scaling c ↦ (v_i c_i)_i. GRS(α, k, 1) = reedSolomon α k.
hypotheses: All v i ≠ 0; α injective and k ≤ #ι in the theorems.
proofSteps: Define generalizedReedSolomon α k v := Submodule.map (diagonal scaling by v) (reedSolomon α k).
Diagonal scaling by a vector of units is a linear isomorphism preserving hammingNorm, so dimension, minimum weight and MDS transfer from reed-solomon-code, reed-solomon-is-mds.

nodes.title: The dual of a GRS code is a GRS code
nodes.statement: Let α : ι → F be injective, n = #ι, k ≤ n and v : ι → F with all v i ≠ 0. Put u_i = (v_i ∏_{j≠i}(α_i − α_j))^{−1}. Then the Euclidean dual (the orthogonal of the dot-product form, AlgebraicCodingTheory Layer 2's C^⊥) of GRS(α, k, v) is GRS(α, n − k, u).
hypotheses: α injective; k ≤ n; v i ≠ 0; the dual is taken for the bilinear form ⟨x, y⟩ = ∑ x_i y_i (no conjugation).
proofSteps: It suffices to show ∑_i u_i v_i p(α_i) q(α_i) = 0 for deg p < k, deg q < n − k, then compare dimensions k + (n − k) = n (the dual has dimension n − k).

h = pq has degree ≤ n − 2; by Lagrange interpolation h = ∑_i h(α_i) L_i with L_i = ∏_{j≠i}(X − α_j)/∏_{j≠i}(α_i − α_j) (mathlib:Lagrange.basis), and the X^{n−1}-coefficient of h, which is 0, equals ∑_i h(α_i)/∏_{j≠i}(α_i − α_j) = ∑_i u_i v_i h(α_i).
acceptance: For α enumerating F_q, ∏_{j≠i}(α_i − α_j) = −1 for every i (the derivative of X^q − X is −1), so the dual of RS(α, k) is RS(α, q − k) (full-length-reed-solomon-dual).
k = 0: the dual of ⊥ is ⊤ = GRS(α, n, u).

nodes.title: Full-length Reed–Solomon codes are dual to each other
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements and α an enumeration of F (α : F → F the identity, ι = F). Then the Euclidean dual of reedSolomon α k is reedSolomon α (q − k) for 0 ≤ k ≤ q; in particular RS(α, q/2) is self-dual when q is even.
hypotheses: F finite; α bijective onto F.
proofSteps: ∏_{j≠i}(α_i − α_j) = f′(α_i) for f = ∏_j (X − α_j) = X^q − X, whose derivative is qX^{q−1} − 1 = −1; so u_i = −1/v_i = −1 for v = 1 and dual-of-generalized-reed-solomon gives GRS(α, q − k, −1) = RS(α, q − k).
Alternative: ∑_{x∈F} x^j = 0 for 0 ≤ j < q − 1 (mathlib:FiniteField.sum_pow_lt_card_sub_one) applied to products of monomials of degree < k and < q − k.
acceptance: Over F₂ (q = 2): RS(α, 1) (repetition) is self-dual.
Over F₃: RS(α, 1)^⊥ = RS(α, 2), the sum-zero code.

nodes.title: Reed–Solomon codes on the multiplicative group are cut out by power-sum checks
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements, n = q − 1, γ a generator of Fˣ, α_i = γ^i (i < n) and 1 ≤ k ≤ n. Then reedSolomon α k = {c ∈ F^n : ∑_{i<n} c_i γ^{iℓ} = 0 for 1 ≤ ℓ ≤ n − k}.
hypotheses: F finite; γ generates Fˣ; α_i = γ^i.
proofSteps: ⊆: for c_i = p(γ^i) with p = ∑_{j<k} p_j X^j, ∑_i c_i γ^{iℓ} = ∑_j p_j ∑_i γ^{i(j+ℓ)}, and ∑_{i<n} γ^{is} = 0 unless n ∣ s; here 1 ≤ j + ℓ ≤ n − 1.
Equality by dimension: the n − k check equations are linearly independent (Vandermonde in the distinct γ^ℓ), so the right side has dimension k = finrank of the left (reed-solomon-code).
acceptance: k = n: no check equations, the code is ⊤.

nodes.title: Subfield subcodes
nodes.statement: Let F ⊆ E be fields ([Algebra F E]) and C ≤ E^ι a linear code over E. Its subfield subcode is subfieldSubcode F C := {x ∈ F^ι : (algebraMap F E ∘ x) ∈ C}, an F-linear code (the comap of C, viewed as an F-subspace by restriction of scalars, under the coordinatewise inclusion F^ι → E^ι).
hypotheses: F ⊆ E fields; ι finite; the dimension bound assumes [E : F] = m finite.
proofSteps: Define subfieldSubcode F C := Submodule.comap (coordinatewise algebraMap as an F-linear map) (C.restrictScalars F).
Weight: hammingNorm (algebraMap ∘ x) = hammingNorm x (algebraMap injective), so nonzero codewords of the subfield subcode have weight ≥ the minimum weight of C (ECT Exercise 5.12(1)).

Dimension: C is cut out by n − k E-linear equations; each E-linear equation restricted to F^ι is m F-linear equations (expand in an F-basis of E), so dim_F subfieldSubcode ≥ n − m(n − k) (ECT Exercise 5.12(2)).
acceptance: subfieldSubcode F ⊤ = ⊤ and subfieldSubcode F C = C when E = F.
For E = GaloisField 2 2 and C = span_E {(1, γ)} with γ ∉ F₂ the subfield subcode is ⊥ although C ≠ ⊥.

sources.excerpt: Definition 31. — Consider a finite field Fq and its degree m extension F_{q^m} for some positive integer m. Let C ⊆ F^n_{q^m} be a linear code, the subfield subcode of C is the code: C ∩ F^n_q.

nodes.title: Primitive narrow-sense BCH codes
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements, E a finite extension of degree m, N = #E − 1 = q^m − 1, γ a generator of Eˣ and 2 ≤ δ ≤ N. The (primitive, narrow-sense) BCH code of designed distance δ is bchCode F γ δ := subfieldSubcode F (reedSolomon α (N − δ + 1)) with α_i = γ^i (i < N); equivalently (reed-solomon-check-characterisation) the words c ∈ F^N with ∑_{i<N} c_i γ^{iℓ} = 0 for 1 ≤ ℓ ≤ δ − 1. Length restriction (pinned): n = q^m − 1.
hypotheses: F finite with q elements; E ⊇ F of degree m; γ generates Eˣ; 2 ≤ δ ≤ N.
proofSteps: Define via subfield-subcode and reed-solomon-code.
Check-equation form: reed-solomon-check-characterisation with n − k = δ − 1.
Cyclicity: the check equations are invariant under the cyclic shift c ↦ (c_{i−1 mod N}) (multiplying the ℓ-th check by γ^ℓ).
acceptance: q = 2, m = 3, δ = 3: the binary [7, 4, 3] Hamming code (ECT Exercise 5.11(3)).
m = 1: BCH = RS over F itself with k = N − δ + 1.

nodes.title: The BCH bound
nodes.statement: Every nonzero codeword of bchCode F γ δ has hammingNorm ≥ δ.

nodes.title: Evaluation of functions at a rational place
nodes.statement: Let F/k be a function field (TauCeti.IsFunctionField k F) and P a rational place (P.degree = 1, TauCeti.Place.degree). For f in the valuation ring 𝒪_P (TauCeti.Place.integers P) its value is f(P) := (Place.residueFieldEquivOfDegreeEqOne P h).symm (residue f) ∈ k. Pinned: evalAtRational P h : P.integers →ₐ[k] k is a k-algebra map with kernel the maximal ideal; for functions outside 𝒪_P no value is assigned.
hypotheses: F/k a function field; P a place of degree 1.
proofSteps: Compose the residue map 𝒪_P → F_P (IsLocalRing.residue) with the inverse of the k-algebra isomorphism k ≃ F_P of a rational place (tauceti:TauCeti.Place.residueFieldEquivOfDegreeEqOne).
Kernel = maximal ideal: the residue map has that kernel and the second map is an isomorphism.
evalAtRational (algebraMap k F c) = c: residueFieldEquivOfDegreeEqOne_apply.
acceptance: In k(x), at the place P_{x−a} of the monic irreducible x − a, the value of x is a.
The value of a constant c is c.

nodes.title: Algebraic geometry evaluation codes C_L(D, G)
nodes.statement: Let k be a finite field, F/k a function field with exact constant field k (IsFunctionField k F and IsIntegrallyClosedIn k F), G a divisor, and P_1, …, P_n pairwise distinct rational places not in the support of G; put D = P_1 + ⋯ + P_n. The evaluation code is C_L(D, G) := the image of the k-linear map ev : L(G) → k^n, f ↦ (f(P_1), …, f(P_n)), where L(G) = TauCeti.riemannRochSpace G and f(P_i) is evalAtRational (f ∈ 𝒪_{P_i} because P_i ∉ supp G).
hypotheses: k finite; F/k a function field with exact constants; P_i distinct, of degree 1, G.coeff P_i = 0.
proofSteps: ev is well defined: f ∈ L(G) and G(P_i) = 0 give v_{P_i}(f) ≥ 0 (tauceti:TauCeti.mem_riemannRochSpace_iff), so f ∈ 𝒪_{P_i}; evaluation is k-linear (evaluation-at-rational-place).
Define agEvaluationCode as LinearMap.range ev.
acceptance: For the rational function field and G = (k − 1)P∞ the code is a Reed–Solomon code (reed-solomon-as-ag-code).
If deg G < 0 then L(G) = 0 and C_L = ⊥.

nodes.title: Duality of evaluation and residue codes
nodes.statement: In the setting of algebraic-geometry-evaluation-code (k finite, exact constants): C_Ω(D, G) is the Euclidean dual of C_L(D, G), and finrank C_Ω = n − finrank C_L.
hypotheses: As in algebraic-geometry-evaluation-code.
proofSteps: Orthogonality: for f ∈ L(G) and ω ∈ Ω_F(G − D), the abstract residue theorem gives ∑ᶠ_P ω_P(f) = 0 (tauceti:TauCeti.finsum_repartitionDualComponent_eq_zero).
For P ∉ {P_i}: v_P(f) ≥ −G(P) = −(G − D)(P), so ω_P(f) = 0 (tauceti:TauCeti.repartitionDualComponent_apply_eq_zero_of_le).
At P_i: (G − D)(P_i) = −1 and f − f(P_i) vanishes at P_i, so ω_{P_i}(f − f(P_i)) = 0 and ω_{P_i}(f) = f(P_i)·ω_{P_i}(1) (evaluation-at-rational-place); hence ∑_i f(P_i) ω_{P_i}(1) = 0.

Dimension: the kernel of ω ↦ (ω_{P_i}(1))_i on Ω_F(G − D) is Ω_F(G) (tauceti:TauCeti.mem_weilDifferentialFiltration_iff_repartitionDualComponent_eq_zero, checking the local condition at each P_i), so finrank C_Ω = i(G − D) − i(G) (tauceti:TauCeti.finrank_weilDifferentialFiltration); Riemann–Roch (tauceti:TauCeti.exists_isRiemannRochDivisor with TauCeti.Divisor.indexOfSpecialty) turns this into n − (ℓ(G) − ℓ(G − D)) = n − finrank C_L (ag-code-dimension).
An orthogonal subspace of dimension n − dim C_L is the whole dual.
acceptance: Rational function field with G = (k₀ − 1)P∞ and all q places: the theorem recovers full-length-reed-solomon-dual.
G = 0 over RatFunc k with n points: C_L is the repetition code and C_Ω the sum-zero code.

sources.excerpt: The two constructions are dual to each other (see for instance [123, Th. 2.2.8]): Theorem 12. — The two codes defined just above are dual of each other: CΩ(X, P, G) = CL (X, P, G)⊥.

nodes.title: Parameters of residue codes
nodes.statement: If 2g − 2 < deg G < n then finrank C_Ω(D, G) = n + g − 1 − deg G and every nonzero codeword of C_Ω(D, G) has weight ≥ deg G − (2g − 2).
hypotheses: As in algebraic-geometry-evaluation-code; 2g − 2 < deg G < n.
proofSteps: Dimension: residue-code-is-dual and ag-code-dimension (finrank C_L = deg G + 1 − g).

Distance: let ω ∈ Ω_F(G − D) be nonzero with residue vector c, and S = {i : c_i = 0}. For i ∈ S, ω_{P_i} kills 1 and (as (G − D)(P_i) = −1) every function vanishing at P_i, hence all of 𝒪_{P_i} = k + 𝔪_{P_i}; by tauceti:TauCeti.mem_weilDifferentialFiltration_iff_repartitionDualComponent_eq_zero, ω ∈ Ω_F(B) with B = G − D + ∑_{i∈S} P_i.

Ω_F(B) = 0 when deg B ≥ 2g − 1, since finrank Ω_F(B) = i(B) (tauceti:TauCeti.finrank_weilDifferentialFiltration) and i(B) = 0 in that range (tauceti:TauCeti.Divisor.indexOfSpecialty_eq_zero_of_two_mul_genus_sub_one_le_degree). Hence deg G − n + #S ≤ 2g − 2, i.e. hammingNorm c = n − #S ≥ deg G − 2g + 2.

The bound k + d ≥ n + 1 − g also holds for C_Ω when deg G > 2g − 2.

nodes.title: Terras's finite upper half-plane H_q
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements, q odd, E a field with [Algebra F E] and [E : F] = 2, and s ∈ E with s ∉ F and δ := s² ∈ F (so δ is a nonsquare of F and E = F(s)). The finite upper half-plane is H := {z ∈ E : z ∉ range (algebraMap F E)}; every z ∈ H is uniquely z = x + y s with x ∈ F, y ∈ Fˣ, and Re z := x, Im z := y. Conventions (pinned): 'upper' means y ≠ 0 (Terras's H_q is a double cover of an upper half-plane); Im depends on the chosen s, and replacing s by c s rescales Im by c^{−1}.
hypotheses: F finite, q = #F odd; [E : F] = 2; s ∉ F with s² ∈ F.
proofSteps: Define FiniteUpperHalfPlane F E := {z : E // z ∉ Set.range (algebraMap F E)}.
(1, s) is an F-basis of E (s ∉ F, dimension 2), giving the coordinates x, y; y ≠ 0 iff z ∉ F.
Hence H ≃ F × Fˣ and Nat.card H = q(q − 1).
acceptance: q = 3, δ = −1: H has 6 elements x + y i, y = ±1.
s itself (x = 0, y = 1) and −s lie in H; elements of F do not.

sources.excerpt: Let Fq be a finite field with q elements (q odd.) Fix a non-square elemnet δ ∈ F. Hq = Fq(√δ) − Fq = {x + y√δ | x, y ≠ 0 ∈ Fq} is called the finite Poincaré plane.
sources.match: The definition (with 'elemnet' as printed).

sources.excerpt: We define the finite Poincaré upper half-plane as Hq = {z = x + y√σ : x, y ∈ Fq and y ≠ 0}. Note that “half-plane” is something of a misnomer since y ≠ 0 may not be a good finite analogue of the condition y > 0
sources.match: The convention y ≠ 0.

sources.excerpt: Fix q ≥3 odd and Fq, a finite field of q elements. Suppose δ ∈ Fq is not a square of any element of Fq. Then the finite upper half-plane is said to be the set Hq = {x + y√δ | x ∈ Fq, y ∈ F×q },
sources.match: Same definition.

nodes.title: The fractional linear action of GL(2, F_q) on H_q
nodes.statement: In the setting of finite-upper-half-plane, GL(2, F) acts on H by g · z = (a z + b)/(c z + d) for g = [[a, b], [c, d]]. It is well defined (cz + d ≠ 0 since z ∉ F and (c, d) ≠ (0, 0)), lands in H because Im(g z) = det(g)·Im(z)/N(cz + d) with N = Algebra.norm F, and is a MulAction; scalar matrices act trivially.
hypotheses: As in finite-upper-half-plane.
proofSteps: cz + d = 0 with (c, d) ≠ 0 would put z = −d/c ∈ F (or c = 0 = d).
Im formula: (az + b)/(cz + d) = (az + b)(c z̄ + d)/N(cz + d) and the s-coordinate of (az + b)(cz̄ + d) is (ad − bc)·Im z (z̄ = the Galois conjugate, s ↦ −s).
Action axioms: the usual composition of fractional linear transformations (matrix multiplication), 1 acts trivially.
acceptance: −1 ∈ GL(2, F) acts trivially: the action is not faithful.
